import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 830

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/830](https://www.erdosproblems.com/830)
-/

open scoped ArithmeticFunction.sigma
open Filter Real

namespace Erdos830

open scoped Classical in
/--
Let $A(x)$ counts the number of amicable $1\leq a\leq b\leq x$.
-/
noncomputable abbrev A (x : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  Finset.card <| (Finset.Icc 1 ⌊x⌋₊ ×ˢ Finset.Icc 1 ⌊x⌋₊).filter fun (a, b) ↦
    a ≤ b ∧ IsAmicable a b

/-- **Erdos Problem 830, Part 1**
We say that $a,b\in \mathbb{N}$ are an amicable pair if $\sigma(a)=\sigma(b)=a+b$. Are there
infinitely many amicable pairs?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_830.parts.i : answer(sorry) ↔ {(a, b) | IsAmicable a b}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/-- **Erdos Problem 830, Part 2**
We say that $a,b\in \mathbb{N}$ are an amicable pair if $\sigma(a)=\sigma(b)=a+b$.
If $A(x)$ counts the number of amicable $1\leq a\leq b\leq x$ then is it true that
$$A(x) > x^{1-o(1)}?$$
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_830.parts.ii : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ o : ℝ → ℝ, o =o[atTop] (1 : ℝ → ℝ) ∧ ∀ᶠ x in atTop,
    x ^ (1 - o x) < A x := by
  sorry

/--
We say that $a,b\in \mathbb{N}$ are an amicable pair if $\sigma(a)=\sigma(b)=a+b$.
If $A(x)$ counts the number of amicable $1\leq a\leq b\leq x$ then one can show that $A(x) = o(x)$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_830.variants.erdos : A =o[atTop] id := by
  sorry

/--
We say that $a,b\in \mathbb{N}$ are an amicable pair if $\sigma(a)=\sigma(b)=a+b$.
If $A(x)$ counts the number of amicable $1\leq a\leq b\leq x$ then one can show that
$A(x) \leq x \exp(-(\log x)^{1/3})$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_830.variants.pomerance : ∀ᶠ x in atTop, A x ≤ x * rexp (- Real.nthRoot 3 x.log) := by
  sorry

/--
We say that $a,b\in \mathbb{N}$ are an amicable pair if $\sigma(a)=\sigma(b)=a+b$.
If $A(x)$ counts the number of amicable $1\leq a\leq b\leq x$ then one can show that
$A(x) \leq x \exp(-(\tfrac{1}{2}+o(1))(\log x\log\log x)^{1/2})$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_830.variants.pomerance_stronger :
    ∃ o : ℝ → ℝ, o =o[atTop] (1 : ℝ → ℝ) ∧
    ∀ᶠ x in atTop, A x ≤ x * rexp (- (1/ 2 + o x) * √(x.log * x.log.log)) := by
  sorry

end Erdos830

findings.description: The filter uses `a ≤ b ∧ IsAmicable a b`, but `IsAmicable` contains only the two sigma equations, without distinctness. Consequently A counts every positive perfect number as a diagonal pair. Lean checks prove `A 6 = 1` and `A 284 = 3`; the distinct-amicable-pair counts are respectively 0 and 1. This conflicts with the definition in the primary literature. However, the immediate source webpage itself omits distinctness from its sigma-only definition and writes `a ≤ b`, so the existing definition is defensible as a literal reading of that page. The intended convention needs clarification.
findings.source_evidence: Pomerance, On amicable numbers (2015), §1: “Two different positive integers a, b with s(a) = b and s(b) = a are said to form an amicable pair” (https://math.dartmouth.edu/~carlp/amicablesv3.pdf). The Wikipedia article linked from problem 830 likewise specifies “two different natural numbers” (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amicable_numbers). Erdős–Dudley (1983), p. 296, discusses the count of pairs m < n < x (https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1983-27.pdf). In contrast, https://www.erdosproblems.com/830 gives only the sigma equations.
findings.suggested_fix: For the conventional problem, replace `a ≤ b` by `a < b` in A, or add distinctness to the shared amicability predicate. Document distinctness and cite the primary definition. If counting perfect-number self-pairs is deliberate, explicitly identify this as an extended counting function rather than silently using the conventional name.

findings.description: Independently of A, this theorem also lacks distinctness. I proved in Lean that its right-hand side is equivalent to `(infinitely many distinct amicable pairs) ∨ (infinitely many perfect numbers)`. Thus infinitude of perfect numbers alone would provide a positive answer to the formal question, whereas the primary literature asks for infinitely many distinct amicable pairs. This is not merely the harmless use of ordered pairs or the inclusion of zero. As with A, the sigma-only definition on the immediate webpage supports a more permissive interpretation, so this is a source-convention concern rather than an unambiguous transcription error.
findings.source_evidence: Erdős–Dudley, Some remarks and problems in number theory related to the work of Euler (1983), p. 296, defines the counting problem using m < n < x and conjectures infinitely many such pairs (https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1983-27.pdf). Pomerance (2015), §1, explicitly requires “two different positive integers” before stating that their infinitude is unknown (https://math.dartmouth.edu/~carlp/amicablesv3.pdf). The immediate webpage, https://www.erdosproblems.com/830, omits that requirement in its displayed definition.
findings.suggested_fix: For the conventional question, use `answer(sorry) ↔ {p : ℕ × ℕ | p.1 < p.2 ∧ IsAmicable p.1 p.2}.Infinite`, or require `p.1 ≠ p.2`. Alternatively, explicitly label the existing statement as the question allowing perfect-number self-pairs and distinguish it from the original problem.

findings.description: The Lean exponent contains `√(x.log * x.log.log)`, whereas the named 2015 Pomerance theorem contains √(log x · log log log x). The missing logarithm gives a substantially stronger upper bound: the ratio of the square-root factors tends to infinity, so the difference cannot be absorbed into a coefficient `1/2 + o(1)`. The Lean statement and docstring do accurately reproduce the double-log formula currently displayed on erdosproblems.com/830; the concern is that this secondary-source formula disagrees with the primary theorem it attributes to Pomerance.
findings.source_evidence: Pomerance, On amicable numbers (2015), Theorem 1.1, author PDF p. 2: `#𝒜(x) ≤ x / exp((1/2 + o(1)) √(log x log log log x))`. Section 3 repeats the triple-log expression in the definition of L(x) and the concluding estimates (https://math.dartmouth.edu/~carlp/amicablesv3.pdf; published citation DOI 10.1007/978-3-319-22240-0_19). The remarks at https://www.erdosproblems.com/830 instead display the double-log formula used by Lean.
findings.suggested_fix: To state Pomerance's Theorem 1.1, replace `√(x.log * x.log.log)` with `√(x.log * x.log.log.log)` and correct the docstring accordingly. Cite the primary theorem directly. Retaining the stronger expression would require a separate supporting reference.

reformulations.difference: Relative to the primary literature's distinct-pair convention, the formal counting function additionally counts perfect-number self-pairs. Nevertheless, this addition does not change the near-linear lower-bound question.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Write A(x) = C(x) + D(x), where C counts distinct pairs and D counts perfect numbers. The classical bound D(x) = O(√x) makes D negligible compared with x^(1-o(1)). If A(x) > x^(1-o(x)) with o(x) → 0, then eventually C(x) > (1/2)x^(1-o(x)) = x^(1-o'(x)), where o'(x) = o(x) + log(2)/log(x) → 0. The converse follows from C ≤ A. Thus the definition concern does not produce a separate mathematical mismatch in this theorem.

reformulations.difference: The formal A includes perfect-number self-pairs, unlike the distinct-pair interpretation in the primary sources.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: With A = C + D as above and D(x) = O(√x), one has D(x) = o(x). Therefore A(x) = o(x) if and only if C(x) = o(x). The diagonal contribution does not change this density-zero claim.

sources_consulted: Erdős, On amicable numbers, Publ. Math. Debrecen 4 (1955), 108–111: https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1955-03.pdf
Erdős–Dudley, Some remarks and problems in number theory related to the work of Euler, Math. Mag. 56 (1983), 292–298, especially p. 296: https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1983-27.pdf
Pomerance, On amicable numbers (2015), §1, Theorem 1.1 and §3: https://math.dartmouth.edu/~carlp/amicablesv3.pdf
Published abstract and bibliography for Pomerance (2015): https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/978-3-319-22240-0_19
Nguyen–Pomerance, The reciprocal sum of the amicable numbers, Math. Comp. 88 (2019), 1503–1526, Introduction: https://math.dartmouth.edu/~carlp/mcom3362.pdf
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_number — Euclid–Euler form, odd-perfect-number structure, and the O(√x) counting bound under Minor results
review.notes:
The displayed formulas on the immediate Erdős Problems webpage match the Lean file. The three findings are deliberately labelled questionable because they identify conflicts between that summary and its primary references, not clear transcription errors relative to the webpage alone. There are two underlying concerns: distinctness, affecting A and part i separately, and the logarithm in the strongest bound.

All declarations, answer slots, quantifiers and relevant definitions were checked. The real little-o-to-one condition means convergence to zero; the eventual bounds avoid problematic logarithm/root inputs. The extra zero pair and ordering of pairs do not affect infinitude. Independent Lean checks in /workspace/review/scratch.lean, equivalences.lean and boundaries.lean compile successfully. They establish the small counts, exact counting-set membership, the perfect-number diagonal characterization, and the infinitude-disjunction equivalence. The latter uses no sorry axioms. The reviewed file remains unchanged.

No independent stale-status issue was found: the source still records the two questions as open and the intended upper bounds as established. The possible correction to the strongest bound is a source-statement correction, not evidence of a recent change in research status.
